noi_dung:
Investigate the Hua-tou: Using a Discursive Thought to Subdue Discursive Thoughts

The Chan Session is about to begin.

In the Chan Hall we do not recite the Buddha's name; during a Buddha-recitation Session we do not investigate Chan. Now, we must "walk in Chan, sit in Chan, stand in Chan, lie down in Chan"—in short, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, we investigate Chan.

In the past, one who investigated Chan never gave rise to a single thought; that is called "no thought":

When not a single thought arises, the whole is revealed.

When the six senses suddenly stir, it is covered by clouds.

(When not a single thought arises, the whole (the true mind) appears.

When the six senses suddenly stir, (the Buddha-nature) is covered by clouds.)

To investigate Chan is to investigate "not a single thought arising." It was not until the Ming dynasty that people adopted the method of "investigating the hua-tou." Nowadays every Chan Hall investigates the hua-tou. There are many kinds of hua-tou, such as "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" or "Before my parents gave birth to me, what did my face look like?" or "What is 'nothing'?" and so on.

To investigate Chan is to give rise to no discursive thoughts at all. For example, when investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" you keep reflecting, seeking to find who it is that recites the Buddha's name. But in fact this too is just a discursive thought; it is only that we use one discursive thought to control all other discursive thoughts. This method is called "using the false to control the false, using poison to counter poison." Even reciting "Amitabha Buddha" is "using the false to control the false"; that is, the thought of reciting the Buddha is false, not real. And even the thought investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name" is false—but this one discursive thought has the power to control all other discursive thoughts. That is the principle of investigating Chan.

One who investigates Chan "kills the Buddha when a Buddha comes, kills the demon when a demon comes," attached to no state at all. When your investigation reaches the point where "above, you do not know there is sky; below, you do not know there is earth; in between, you do not know there are people; outside, you do not know there are things; within, you do not know there is mind," then you will merge into one with the Dharma Realm and may suddenly become enlightened. Remember: do not be swayed by the dust of sound (outer conditions), do not look east and gaze west, and do not let your mind waver and scatter!

When your Chan investigation reaches "no self, no others, no living beings, no life," you will sever the root of birth and death and will meet Shakyamuni Buddha face to face—only then will you know the wonder of investigating Chan.

From limitless kalpas until today, we are truly fortunate to have met the Dharma-door of "joining a Chan Session." Therefore we must be especially single-minded, sincere and earnest, and apply effort vigorously; do not squander precious time, do not idle away thoughts on food, clothing, or lodging, for "a moment of time is a moment of life"—time and life are equally precious:

An inch of time, an inch of gold;

An inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

An inch of gold lost is easily regained;

Time once gone is hard to find again.

Meaning:

An inch of time is an inch of gold,

Yet an inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

An inch of gold lost is still easily found,

But time slipped away is hard to seek again.

This poem speaks of the preciousness of time in ordinary days—how much more precious is time during a Session.

No one knows in which minute or second they will become enlightened; therefore, make use of every second and minute—do not waste them. I hope all who join this Chan Session will be valiant and vigorous, never lax or indulgent. Only by enduring every hardship will you attain bliss. To bear what others can hardly bear, to endure what others can hardly endure—that is the spirit of cultivating the Way!

(Explained in September 1975 at Gold Mountain Monastery)
